front: What do Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms both compute?
back: The Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of a connected, undirected, weighted graph.

front: Kruskal's algorithm: what data structure detects cycles, and what dominates its time complexity?
back: A Union-Find (Disjoint-Set) structure detects cycles; the O(E log E) sort of edges dominates overall complexity.

front: Is Kruskal edge-centric or vertex-centric? Prim?
back: Kruskal is edge-centric (processes edges globally sorted by weight). Prim is vertex-centric (grows one tree from a start vertex), structurally similar to Dijkstra.

front: Prim's algorithm: what is the start vertex's key initialized to in this course, and why not just 0?
back: −∞ — a pure sentinel guaranteeing the start vertex is extracted first regardless of other keys. (0 happens to also work when all weights are positive, but −∞ is the general-purpose choice, and matches the course's reference implementation's actual constant name.)

front: Kruskal and Prim: how are ties (equal edge weight, or equal key value) broken in this course?
Exam-tested distinguishing fact: can Prim's intermediate result ever be a disconnected forest?
back: No — Prim always grows exactly ONE connected tree from the start vertex, so its intermediate state is never disjoint. Kruskal, by contrast, routinely holds several disjoint tree fragments mid-run. A disconnected partial edge set immediately rules out Prim.

front: If a graph has one edge of strictly minimum weight, what can you say about it?
back: It belongs to EVERY minimum spanning tree of that graph (exchange-argument proof: any MST excluding it could be strictly improved by swapping it in).

front: If all edge weights in a graph are pairwise distinct, what can you say about its MST?
back: It is unique — a direct consequence of the 'unique cheapest edge is always in the MST' fact applied repeatedly.
